utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness H. Will you please stand up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall call you Witness H because of the protective measures granted to you. You will now take the solemn declaration, which the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can take your seat now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you living a happy life, Witness H?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the inscription "Have a happy life," you are trying to make it happy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a present from a colleague in Austria, but I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whatever the case, your friend knew that you needed that. Very well. You will now look at this piece of paper and just tell us yes or no, that is, whether this is your name or not on this piece of paper. Only yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness H, thank you very much for coming here to testify. You will now answer questions which Mr. McCloskey, the Prosecutor, will ask of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, can you first tell us how old you are?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I grew up in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us where you were living on July 11th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: In Potocari, near Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were you living with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: With my wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you decide that day to go to the UN compound at some time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Because I could not go through the forest, and so I decided that I would be safer with the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was happening that caused you and others to go to Potocari and some others to go through the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Some, that is, the troops mostly, went through the woods, and the civilians, by and large, went to Potocari, to be under the UNPROFOR protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say "the troops went through the woods," you're referring to the Bosnian Muslim troops; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you tell us why the people, why the Muslims, felt a need to either go through the woods or go to Potocari? Why were they fleeing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: They had to. There was no life for them there. We would have all been slain had we stayed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: We were afraid of the Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about what time did you and your family get to the area of the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: About 4.00, 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you take your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: To the Transport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the Transport Factory that had all the old buses in front of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you actually go inside the building of the Transport Company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many other people were inside the building that afternoon that you went there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: You mean both men and women?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, everybody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you spend the night there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you and the other people feeling that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: We all felt bad. We were all afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next day, in the morning, what happened in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: In the morning, around 10.00, I think, Serb troops came in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what those troops were wearing, what kind of outfits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Multicoloured, military clothes. Yellow and green, different colours. Yellow and green clothes. Serb troops. They had round patches on their arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the round thing you saw on their arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Those were round patches; blue, white, red.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know what that meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I knew it meant Serb military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you first saw these Serb military soldiers, where were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: They were behind the Transport Bus Company, and I was watching them through the window. They were in front of the Transport door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were still inside the building, watching these troops through the window.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about what time was this again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It could have been 10.00 or so, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see any of the soldiers that you recognised around that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I saw Goran Rakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his father's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Momcilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was he from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Zalazje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how old was Goran Rakic at the time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: About 22, 23.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Military, multicoloured clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Just standing with other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the other soldiers that he was standing with dressed like him and armed like him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: They were, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what else happened that morning? As the day went on, what else did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I saw a van come and take away Ibrahim Mustafic and a couple of other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the van arrived, who actually took Ibran Mustafic and put him in the van? Could you tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I can't because I was lying down, and I had almost my eyes shut as those soldiers came through -- went through with their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you decide to do anything when you saw these soldiers and Goran Rakic, and Ibran Mustafic taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I decided to pretend I was mad and unable to move about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your family and friends around you assist in this act or charade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes, and those women who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did any soldiers come in and confront you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Two soldiers in black clothes came, and they had bandannas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you when the two soldiers in black came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I was lying down in that passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you acting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Like a man who was disabled and mad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the soldiers do when they saw you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: They came close to me and said, "Come on. Stand up."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: And the women said, "He cannot stand up; he's disabled and he's mad, and he can't move."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so what did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Then one came close to me, and I just slightly opened my eyes, and he took something -- I can't really say what it was -- something which looked like scissors and passed it over my nose, and I still have a scar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, for the record, you pointed at the bridge of your nose and passed your finger over your nose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The record should also indicate that the witness does have a scar where he pointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the soldiers say anything when they did this to your nose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: They said, "Let him be. We'll be back."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what's the next thing -- what did you do after the soldiers cut you like this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Then women found some kerchiefs to stop the bleeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And eventually did you leave that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: When people began to go out of the Transport, we all left the Transport because it was not safe there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you decide it wasn't safe there, besides getting cut by soldiers? Anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Women were crying, "Yes, let's get out of here. Let's get out," and everybody did get out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about what time of day was it when you and your family got out of the bus transport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It could have been around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I went behind the Transport, because there were more people there and other people also started there, so I went along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of area was behind the Transport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It was a meadow, and there was some maize.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you -- how long were you behind the Transport, in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Some 10, maybe 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see anything happening nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I saw a machine, a tractor or something. I wasn't particularly keen on checking that. And I saw dead, heaped one on top of the other. And there were some more soldiers behind them, and I recognised Mr. Milisav Gavric, a former policeman in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many dead did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I should say some 20 to 30 pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you see any injuries to those dead people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I could see they were lying one on top of the other, but I could see that they had -- that their necks had been slit, cut, behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe, if you recall, what this machine that you've described as a tractor was doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, it looked like a tractor. I wasn't really paying much attention, because when I saw all those dead, it seemed -- or perhaps it was an excavator or something like that. It was digging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe what Milisav Gavric was wearing and what he was doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: He was wearing blue/grey police clothes and he had a dog on a leash.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did he have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Over his shoulder, I couldn't really see much more, I only saw that he had it over his shoulder. I couldn't see the type.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you watch this scene that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: A minute or two. Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, then, when I saw Milisav Gavric there and those men with their necks cut, then we went back to the Transport building. But we went up towards the janitor's building, facility, where UNPROFOR had a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall last night looking at a photograph of the Transport Company and marking on it where you saw these bodies and this tractor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, here is a photocopy of the photograph that you marked last night. And could you take that pointer in front of you and tell us what those marks are and point to them on the photograph. Just look directly at the photograph, not the screen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I was here [indicates], and here was that tractor or excavator, or whatever. And those dead, with their necks cut, were here [indicates], and Gavric was here too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're pointing to a little circle on the right-hand side of the screen with those little marks, and those marks represent the tractor, the bodies, and the soldiers, including Gavric. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes, and some soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the other witness's microphone be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we switch the other microphone on so the interpretation can hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other area that's marked with a little "W," did you mark that last night as the area you witnessed this from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you with your family at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. My wife was there too, and my two children, and there were other people too, women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were hiding somewhere in that vicinity, watching this tractor and the bodies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd also like to show the witness Exhibit 69.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember speaking with an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor somewhere around November 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time did you have a chance to draw a diagram of the area where you saw the tractor and the bodies and the Transport Company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Exhibit 69 that's in front of you, is that a copy of your drawing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain the drawing a little bit? Point out what the various things are on it and what they mean, around the tractor and where you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: So Milisav Gavric was here [indicates]; bodies were here [indicates]; and the tractor, right next to those bodies, that tractor, that machine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. For the record, you indicated the initials "MG" was where Milisav Gavric was, and then the little circle is where the tractor was, and the bodies are next to that. You've written all those behind the Transport Company; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you said after seeing this scene and Milisav Gavric, you left and went back to the Transport Company. And where exactly did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I went to where the buses were, in front of the janitor's house, where UNPROFOR vehicles were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, there were lots of people there, quite a number of men. The compound was full of people, of women and children and men, and they were all moving closer to UNPROFOR so as to get protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That day did you see any other Serb soldiers or personnel that you knew from before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Sure, I did. When they started to coming toward where people were, I started to hide. Women hid me; they spread their pantaloons wide so that they wouldn't see me. I knew all those people well, and I dared not speak out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a person you knew named Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you first see Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: That was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The afternoon of the day that we're talking about now, July 12th, the day that you saw the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was Momir Nikolic when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: He was walking up and down with Jokic, a former policeman, and they had another man with them. He used to work in a shop, the third one. I knew him, but I didn't know his name. And there was also a female with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you say that Momir Nikolic was walking up and down. Where was he walking up and down in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Below those -- behind those UNPROFOR vehicles, where those burnt buses were, where people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he near the asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, some ten metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he wearing? What was Momir Nikolic wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: He had a pair of jeans, a black T-shirt, and he had a moustache.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: We used to be good friends before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened that afternoon and evening? Did you stay in that same location, in front of the Transport, or did you move around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No. I moved only when I would see a Serb. When I'd see a Serb, then I tried to hide so that he wouldn't see me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep up the act that you talked about before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't have to until a Serb actually saw you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you spend the night that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: That night I spent next to that janitor's house, and there were APCs, UN APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe that night, the night of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I can, yes. People were sitting around; some were lying down. I was lying down, and there were more women lying next to me. I took a scarf, a kerchief, of my wife's, and I put it on my head, and I took the child Alma in my arms, and I covered myself with a blanket, up to my neck. And sometime after midnight, I think -- I couldn't sleep because I was too afraid and everything else -- but then they came with torches, with flashlamps, and they were looking and checking and I could hear screams and loud crying. Women were screaming, those screams were horrible, and I could see some men taking men away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell, the people with the flashlights, who those people were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you that. I could not see it. I only saw that it was men taking away men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this go on most of the night, these noises and screams and other things you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, it didn't go on all night long. It lasted for about two or three hours, those screams and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Finally when the sun came up, what did you and your family do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: People started down towards trucks and buses, and I could see that we were among the last ones, that people had already left. So I found, a cart, a wheelbarrow, and I told my wife, "Let's get it." I first looked to see if any of the Serb soldiers or any of the Serbs were looking in my direction, and I saw that nobody did. I managed to stand up and get into this wheelbarrow, and my wife pushed it. And I bent my head down and put my tongue out, I was also unshaven by that time, and I just pretended I was out of my mind, I was mad. And my wife pushed that wheelbarrow to the buses. I saw many Serb troops, and when we were some 30 metres from the buses, a Serb soldier said, "Get him. Fuck your mother and his," and my wife said, "Well, he's sick." And he said, "Never mind that he's sick. To the side with him," so we had to stop. And I told my wife, "Go," and I bent down so they wouldn't see it, and I said, "Go and find an UNPROFOR man." She went to that UNPROFOR man and she was explaining something to him, because she couldn't speak the language, but then she pointed with her finger, pointed her finger at me and the wheelbarrow. And he came then and took up that wheelbarrow and pushed it, with me inside, to Distribucija. [Interpreter's Note: The power distribution company, the interpreter presumes]. There was the Red Cross, and they were extending first aid there. And he lifted me from the wheelbarrow. I fell, since I saw some two Serb soldiers there, and they lifted me onto a bed, and I spent some two hours there. And right below was this Distribucija, and the buses were down there. I could watch on the sly; when I wouldn't see Serb soldiers there, then I would open my eyes and look. And I looked and I saw how women were boarding those buses, and as soon as a man would appear, a Serb soldier would press his rifle at his stomach and shout, "Gold. Gold. Money. Money. Marks. Marks." When somebody would say, "I don't have any, I haven't got any," then they would curse at them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were there UN soldiers around you, protecting you while you were acting out this part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: You mean where the Red Cross was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were soldiers and some doctors, female. I know there were both female and male doctors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where was this area exactly, compared to where people were being loaded onto the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It was in Potocari, near the distribution company, Distribucija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it inside the UN base compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually get inside the compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, at that point, a vehicle arrived and I was put on the trailer, together with my wife and my two children. So we set out in the direction of the base. It was an UNPROFOR vehicle that took me. And across the road, I could see a number of men, also a pile with their belongings. There was a house full of men in the vicinity. And then we reached the base, and I was put in a corridor. They told my wife and children that they could leave, and I stayed there. That night, at dusk, at sunset, I don't know what time it was, but I could see a little bit through a door that was open, Ratko Mladic arrived, together with his escort; there were some people accompanying him. I was lying down at that moment, and he approached me and he started yelling, and he asked me, "Which unit did you belong to?" and I just made this moaning sound, and he just said, "Look at this motherfucker, he's dying." So he cursed my mother simply like that and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Momir Nikolic again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I saw Momir Nikolic, whether it was on the 19th or the 20th, I don't remember, but Momir Nikolic came in together with the Red Cross people. He came to the base where we were accommodated. He was with Brano, a policeman from Bratunac, and they went from patient to patient, from bed to bed. There were a lot of infirm people there, lots of women as well. Brano was carrying a notebook and Momir didn't have anything. They also had some people accompanying them as an escort, and I knew them from Kravica, I mean their escort. So when he came to me, Brano said, "This guy here should be slaughtered immediately. I know him quite well from Bratunac. He's a cunning person." And then Momir said, "I know (redacted)." There was an interpreter there, and a Dutch doctor arrived as well, and the interpreter talked to the doctor. Whether it was Momir or the doctor who saved me at that moment, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were eventually that day transported out with the other sick and wounded and reunited with your family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to show you one more exhibit, which has been marked Exhibit 68. Do you recall that within the last couple of days I played you a video, which, for the record, is our Exhibit 3, and I asked you whether you were able to recognise any of the people in the video. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I remember this one [indicates]. I know him very well but I just can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've just pointed on Exhibit number 68, and could you point one more time so I can see where you pointed at. I'm sorry. Which person do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: This one here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, that's the person on the far left with the backpack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you got a better look at his face on the video, didn't you? It was a little better quality than this photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. I know him well, independent of any photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I know him by sight. I used to see him often in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask a question, if I'm allowed to do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness H. Let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to be asked whether I know this Krstic person here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We were going to ask you that. Just be patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think I can do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see anybody in court here that you recognise from back in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I can see that one over there. That's Krstic, sitting in the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's he wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: He's wearing a suit. I can only see his shoulders, actually. Because I know that man very well. I don't know where I saw him, but I do know him. As soon as I got in the courtroom, I knew immediately. I know him really well but I just cannot remember where from. But I do know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The record should indicate he's identified the defendant, General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Witness H, now you are going to answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Petrusic, who is representing General Krstic here. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness H.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact that you recognised General Krstic has inspired my first question. Do you know General Krstic from way back then? Is he the same person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: You mean whether I know his face?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. I'm perfectly honest with you. I know this man. I don't know where I used to see him but I know him completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you can't remember where you know him from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No, I cannot, but I know that I know him. As soon as I saw him, right away, I knew that it was Krstic. Whether I saw him in Potocari or somewhere else, I can't tell you, but I used to see him. I don't know where, but I used to see him quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were asked this question about the Prosecutor, you yourself volunteered, you said you wanted to say something, and you mentioned the name Vojislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I know that "Krstic" is his last name. If I didn't know his name, I wouldn't know him. But I know him. But this guy on the photograph, for example, I know him very well, but I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the beginning of your testimony, Witness H. The Muslim army, that is, the Muslim men who had taken to the woods, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they gathered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: You mean the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: You mean the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: How would I know that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they had gone through the woods.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers went through the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "the Muslim army," "the Muslim soldiers."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you again: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: How could they be armed? All the weapons had been taken away by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why are you then referring to them as soldiers, as the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, everybody called them that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that army structured? Did they belong to any particular unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No. They were like a civilian army. They didn't have proper uniforms. They had some kind of rifles. We called them army, but they didn't have proper uniforms or weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give any statements prior to this, to the representatives of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, I did in Sarajevo, in 1998, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to show you your statement at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit is marked D9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should take the liberty to ask the witness, on your behalf, something that you also tell the witness in this case, to pause before giving his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well, Mr. Petrusic. Thank you very much for the attention you're paying to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, after I have asked my question, could you please wait a couple of seconds so that the interpreters can translate the question for the Chamber. I'm referring to your statement of the 27th of November, 1998. It is your statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4 of that statement, the third paragraph from the bottom, let me read you the first sentence of this paragraph: "Near to Gavric I also saw a red-coloured digger, making a hole, and next to this I saw a pile of approximately 40 or 50 dead bodies."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: You expect me to answer? Is that a question? Well, it is very difficult for you to understand me. I was terribly afraid. I saw this machine, I saw this excavator, I wasn't sure it was an excavator, and I saw dead bodies, but they were on a pile. At that moment, I panicked and I became sick from that panic and from the fear, and I'm still suffering from the stress that I experienced at that moment. So don't tell me about that. I mean, do you understand that there are people doing such evil things? It's probably difficult for you to imagine that. But those people had to be defended, whereas they were actually doomed to disappear from the face of the earth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, I do understand the suffering you have been through.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not debating here with the witness. Let me stress once again that I do understand the suffering most of the witnesses have been through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Petrusic. Witness H, please, if you can, try to answer the question put to you by Mr. Petrusic, because you also have to understand that he has a job to do here. So I kindly ask you to answer directly to the questions by Mr. Petrusic. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness H. Mr. Petrusic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, you can distinguish between an excavator and a tractor, can you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, sir, at that moment, I cannot tell you exactly. When I saw the machine, it was a tractor or an excavator. I spent perhaps one minute or two observing those bodies. And immediately after that, I started running away. People were in a panic, they didn't know where to go. There were rumours about slaughters being committed at various places. So people panicked, and we no longer knew where to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know Ibran Mustafic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. We went to school together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us who took him away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you that. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also knew, or rather had an opportunity to see on TV or in the media, photographs of General Mladic and of Arkan as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of Arkan as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, the one that you have in front of you, you say that General Mladic and Arkan came together and they passed you on their way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing civilian clothes and a tie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. So he was wearing civilian clothes and he had a tie. Mladic was standing next to me and Arkan was standing next to Mladic, and I could see his face. I had seen him on TV and in the media, so I thought it was Arkan. I was not 100 per cent sure, but he looked like Arkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, judging from what I had seen on TV and in the media, I could tell it was him. He had a pretty face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, in that area you saw Serb soldiers for the first time, if I correctly understand your statement, from the window of the house where you were staying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was at that time that you could observe their insignia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away from you were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I could see them through my window, and I think that they were between seven and ten metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of their insignia, the one that would indicate which army it was, could you be more specific as to its dimensions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It was round in shape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the perimeter of that -- what would be the perimeter -- the diameter, sorry, of that badge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, at that moment, I didn't know. I wasn't really interested, wasn't paying too much attention to that. I wasn't interested in finding out about the dimensions of the badge. I could only see them. I didn't bother observing it for a long time. I cannot tell you anything about the diameter of the badge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, once again, I do understand the fear that you experienced at that time, but you see, you are now testifying and you obviously had some basis for your conclusions as to the insignia. So I would like to know whether you can be a little more precise, a little closer in your description.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean by "precision"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm interested in the colours, for example. You saw that the badge was red, white, and blue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything written on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. I think something was written in yellow letters, like this [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to see the badge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to this statement, the one that's been shown to you, did you ever give a statement to the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the State Commission for Gathering Facts on War Crimes in the Territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No, I did not. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness H, I suppose you have seen programmes about Srebrenica on television.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: To be perfectly honest with you, I simply couldn't watch it, because after the fall of Srebrenica, after what I had seen -- and I'm telling you this as a man -- after all the stress I was exposed to, I simply couldn't watch it anymore because I have to experience it all over again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few days ago, when you arrived here, did you have an opportunity to see the film at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. I saw photographs, pictures, of the soldiers I could recognise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Krstic on those photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. I did not notice Stanislav Krstic. I said Vojislav, but it's actually Stanislav. No, I couldn't notice him. I cannot tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you shown --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was shown a number of photographs. I was shown one photograph, and I recognised Krstic, Stanislav Krstic. But, simply, I cannot remember. I don't remember if I remember him for some good reasons or for some bad reasons. I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are referring to Stanislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no more questions to ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. McCloskey, will there be any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness H, look at me here. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want from you very brief answers because you have been very clear. We just understood that you acted as a mad man and as a sick man to avoid being, as you said, slaughtered. So I could have drawn two conclusions from that: that you thought, you or the people in the place, thought that everybody, every man would be slaughtered except the sick or the mad. Was that the general idea, the general rumour at that time, on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, you know, I feigned madness because I thought nobody wants to hurt a fool, you know. And those people could not stay there, because I think that half of the people would have stayed there if Serbs left them alone, but people simply couldn't stay there because nobody could stay and stay alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the idea which you all believed is that nobody can stay alive in Srebrenica. Already you knew that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew that. I knew that nobody could stay alive in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And what made you think that? What made you think already that? Because that was even before anything happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Because from the moment the war started, I thought -- I had quite a number of Serb friends. There were more Serbs among my friends than Muslims, because I was mostly pals with Serbs. And then when I saw, "Oh, they want a war," then these friends didn't even want to know me anymore. And then one couldn't but realise that there was no more life for us there once the war broke out. And from what I could hear about all these slaughters, about all the killings, from the beginning of the war, around in different villages, how they killed people, how they slit children's throats and all that, as a man, I've lost many people around me; however, I did not have any losses in my family. I have two brothers but none of them were killed, you know. But still ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I understood. But in addition to what you were watching, was the media, the Serb media, propagating the fear that Muslims would be cleansed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, there were stories about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In the media? Do you know what the media is, the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes, in the media, they were all saying "Serb Srebrenica" on the radio. We didn't have much power, really, at our disposal. We could -- we had some makeshift power stations, we had the streams, so we managed with some generators to listen to the radio. And there were all sorts of statements, such as, "The world is feeding you. The world is feeding you to make you -- to fatten you so that we can slaughter you better," for instance, you could hear things like that on a Serb station, a Serb radio station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you said that you pretended you were mad, the soldiers saw you and passed the scissors and left a scar on your nose. What did they do with the other men, the other people? What did they do with the others? Did they also try to pass scissors or cut things, or what did they do with them? Or were they just playing with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: You mean in that compound where I was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I really couldn't see anything. Why did they do it to me? I don't know. Whether they were just playing with me, whether they really wanted to cut off my nose, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, we come to the -- at 11.00, when you went behind the Transport Company, on the meadow, you saw, as you said, between 20 and 30 dead people, with their necks cut. How far were you from them? Was the vision very clear? Could you see they were dead with their necks cut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Let me tell you, I had a good view. I can't tell you exactly to a millimetre, but it was -- I was some 20 to 30 metres away, you see, so I could see it. I saw people lying down in a heap, and I -- you know, I saw them lie down and I could see those wounds here [indicates]. They were not decapitated, not altogether, but their necks, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And it was already there, done. It was already accomplished, or was this man Gavric still doing something? You said he had a dog and was walking around. What was he doing? Was he continuing the slaughter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I didn't see. I didn't see that. I didn't see that he went on to slaughter anyone. I can't say what I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So what was he doing? You saw him with a dog going around. Could you see anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No, I just saw some more soldiers, and Gavric with the dog on a leash, standing there. And I only watched it for a minute or two, because when I saw Gavric and all that, you know, I simply had to think how to get away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you had the very clear idea that it was done, this killing was done, by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It couldn't have been done by anybody else.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Who could it be? Who else could do something like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you spent the night in the janitor's house -- next to the janitor's house, you heard women screaming and men taken away with flashlamps. Did you understand why the women were screaming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I only heard them screaming. "Brothers, help us. They're taking all our men away." They were sobbing and screaming, and I was terribly afraid because they came with those flashlights. They came up to me, but I had this child in my arms and had this scarf on my head, and they searched with a flashlight. They came with a flashlight up to me, but I was covered and I had the child in my arms, so perhaps they thought that I was a female, so they left me alone. I don't know. Except in the morning, when I got up, I saw that men were gone. I could see a couple of elderly men, but all those men that I saw the day before and the evening before, in the morning they were gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said they were selecting with a flashlamp. Was there any order in the selection? Were they looking for some people, or were they just taking anybody, except, of course, women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, from what I could see, from where I was, that is, near me, any man that was near me, young or old, all those men were gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And finally, you spoke of when you had female doctors around you, when you were taken. These female doctors belonged to what? Were they Serb female doctors? Were the Serbs having their doctors too, to look after the wounded? Or were they Red Cross? What were they, these female doctors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Oh, that was -- I saw two of them. I think they came from the Red Cross. They spoke Serbo-Croatian, I think. [Interpreter's Note: Witness said, "They did not speak Serbo-Croat"]. They were extending aid there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Extending aid to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, to the wounded or what? Since they were wounding them and slaughtering them. What were their doctors doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I saw them dress some wounds. They also dressed the wounds of some women, because there were women there too. When I saw those two Serb soldiers, I again closed my eyes. I mean, as soon as I would see a Serb soldier, I would close my eyes and put my tongue out and pretend I was crazy and paralysed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Finally, why did Momir -- you said Momir saved you, although Brano wanted to slaughter you. Was he a friend of yours? How were you saved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly, but in truth, Brano said, "Oh, we have to slaughter him immediately," and Momir said, "No, I know him," and he was a great friend of mine. Yes, we were really close friends. Now, whether Momir saved me, or was it the Dutch doctor, I don't -- I can't tell you exactly. But somehow I think that it was Momir, if he wanted to, and he might have done it. I think -- it is my impression it was Momir who saved me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We are very happy that you are alive and to see you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. I also have a few questions for you. You said that when you entered this courtroom, you recognised something, Vojislav or General Krstic. You said something like that. Did you see him somewhere, sometime before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Your Honour, I was wrong. I said Vojislav, but he's not Vojislav, he's Stanislav Krstic. I don't know. I really saw that man a number of times. I mean, I just know his face. His face is very familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I don't question your conclusion. All I want to know is how did you arrive that conclusion? And if you could answer my questions precisely. Did you, at least once, see General Krstic, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I really -- I'm really telling you, I don't know where I saw that man, but his face is so familiar to me, but I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know, what did he do for a living? What was his profession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you remember what he wore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I can't tell you. All I can say is that I saw him in civilian clothes. Really, I cannot really say -- burden my soul by saying I saw something that I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Witness H. As I said, I'm not questioning your conclusions. But you saw him then wearing civilian clothes before you entered this courtroom or after you entered this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: The first time, when this gentleman showed me Krstic's photograph, I said, "I know the man. I really know him." And as soon as I entered the courtroom, I immediately recognised him. As soon as I came through this door, I looked and I knew it was him. I just know that name, I know that face, but I really, for the life of me, can't remember where I saw the man, where it was. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand very well, Witness H. It happens to me too, that in the street, I can identify a person whom I saw only on a photograph. All I wanted to know was where did you come to know him. I do not doubt your conclusions. But what I can then conclude is that you never met in a coffee shop or in the street or in some office or building, anything, and you simply have that image in your mind somewhere; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: From what I think, I used to see Mr. Krstic in Milici; that is, now, when I think back, I think it was in Milici that I used to see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're already becoming more concrete. It seems to you, you think that it could have been in Milici that you saw General Krstic. Would you remember the setting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I had a friend in Milici and would go to visit him there, and I spent a lot of time there. And I think, I don't really know, I won't know where that man came from or who he was or what he was, but then I heard rumours that he'd been declared a war criminal, or anything. That is what I heard. But I never heard any information about him or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milici, you say, is where perhaps you might have seen him. Was it at night-time or in daytime? Was he alone or in the company of somebody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Daytime. But again I must repeat it. Please don't understand me wrongly. It could have been in Potocari among the troops, when the soldiers were there. It could have been there too. But somehow I think that I used to see him wearing civilian clothes, and in Milici. I'm telling you what I really think and what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well, Witness H. You told Judge Riad that there was a Serb radio station which said all sorts of things. Was there a Muslim radio station as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: In Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how about television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: We watched only Serb television, I mean, a Serb programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Serb radio station and the Serb television were the ones which you could watch in Srebrenica, and they belonged to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. A month earlier, on television I watched when that -- what was his name? It slips my mind -- when he said that he would disarm the Muslims and kill them all. Radovan Karadzic. Radovan Karadzic, he was the one who said it. I knew I had it somewhere. I couldn't remember it for a moment. A month before Srebrenica fell, he said, "I will disarm the Muslims in Srebrenica and kill them all," the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that Radovan Karadzic said that a month before Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: A month before. A month before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And you could hear statements of that nature every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. You told us about screams and sobbing of women during the night. Those cries, those screams, were they real or had they been recorded, perhaps? Would you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, no. That was happening. That was real. They were crying, they were indeed crying, because when so many women begin to cry, I don't know, if I had any power to dig a hole with my hands and hide in that hole, that is how I felt as a man. Because what I experienced, I can't really believe it. I cannot believe that people -- I don't say that all Serbs are like that, but the majority of them, that they could do it to people. You know, a man feels sorry for a beast when he kills it. What kind of human people are they? For instance, that gentleman, Mr. Krstic, if he was responsible to stop that, you know ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Witness H. You are about to finish your testimony, but I think, Mr. Dubuisson, we still have some exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They are Prosecution Exhibits 68, 69, and 70, and for the Defence, D9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. McCloskey, as for 68, 69, and 70, do you have to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On 69, there's a signature that we're not sure exactly whose it is at this point. I might -- we may just out of an abundance of caution excise -- delete it so that if it happens to be the witness's, it's not there. The same thing is true of the statement of the Defence. We have redacted that and can provide it to the registry so that that can be sorted out also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. McCloskey, thank you very much. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we have no objections to any of the Prosecution Exhibits, and we should like to adduce this statement as Exhibit D9, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the necessary redaction, so as to conceal the identity of the witness. Is that what you agree with, Mr. Petrusic? You will agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Mr. Dubuisson, we shall therefore admit into evidence 68, 69, D9, and following the redaction, we shall also have them as publicly accessible versions. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness H, you have now finished your testimony. Thank you very much for coming here. But would you like to add anything that you have not had the opportunity of telling us before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what do you know? If I have anything to add? I wanted to say that those people, those Serbs, it is simply beyond me how they could do it. I don't say all of them are like that, but what kind of people are they? And if Mr. Krstic could put a stop to it and didn't want to, I don't really know who can defend such people, I mean, people who committed such a misdeed. I simply -- it is simply way beyond me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Witness H, but remember that not all the Serbs are like some of them, and I think it holds true of everybody. At any rate, thank you very much for coming here, and I hope that this badge that you have, these words that you have on your jacket, "Happy for life," that it will be communicated to your heart, to your soul, and many other people, be they Serbs or Muslims or Croats, or whatever, that they should always try to have it inscribed on their heart, because everything comes from there. And from this phrase you have, have a happy life.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We shall now make a break. But will the usher help Witness H to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I should like to note that we did mark 70. So we have 68, 69, 70, and D9 as the exhibits entered for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Harmon, before the break, however, who will be our next witness? And where are we now? I mean, in terms of the number of witnesses. How many of them shall we have tomorrow? Several? Or am I being optimistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will start one this afternoon. I don't know, since it is Mr. Cayley's witness, how long that witness will last, and then we have witnesses scheduled for tomorrow, at least one who will be a long witness. And we have evidence to follow that witness in the event it's shorter than I anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the witness whom you shall have after the break, does he need any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was only in view of saving time, to have the preparations necessary. Are we in an open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our only concern is the public sessions, that is, the public needs to now whether it will be a closed or an open session. We need to know that before that, and besides adjustments need to be made. But whatever the case, we shall have a 20-minute break. We shall resume then and we shall have to find out whether we will be working in an open or a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I don't know whether I'm going to pronounce your name correctly. "Van Duijn," more or less.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon. Let us first hear the solemn declaration that the usher will show you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for coming here to testify, Witness. You will first answer questions that are going to be put to you by Mr. Cayley, who is representing the Prosecution. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain van Duijn, from the outset, you speak excellent English but if there is anything you don't understand that I ask you, or that, indeed, the Defence ask you, please do ask for the question to be repeated or clarified. Your name is Captain Leendert van Duijn; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are Dutch by nationality?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you are presently a captain in the Royal Dutch army, serving with the Limburgse Jagers in Germany; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You attended the Royal Military Academy in Breda from 1989 to 1993 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness' second microphone be switched on, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just wait a moment. The second microphone needs to be switched on. You might also actually, if you wish, put the headphones on because the Judges may intervene while I'm questioning you and they will be speaking to you in French. You attended the Royal Military Academy from 1989 to 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think at the end of 1993 you were commissioned into the army as a second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think in November of 1994, you were promoted to a first lieutenant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I think in January of 1995, you deployed to Bosnia with DutchBat III as a platoon commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you also please make a break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's hard, and I'll try to go as slow as I can, to break between my asking you a question and your answering, because there are interpreters between us. How long had you spent with your platoon in the Netherlands training prior to actually going out to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was a period of about six months of training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the average age of the men in your platoon?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Must have been more or less about 19 years old or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were essentially late teenagers who were serving under you.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I was at the time 24, turning 25 in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you deployed to Bosnia, really, as a young officer and a brand new platoon commander in the army.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you now to cast your mind back to July of 1995, and I want to concentrate first on the period of the 9th and 10th of July of 1995. Do you recall where you were at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At that time, I was in a blocking position, south of the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what a blocking position was?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was a position taken by the UN with APCs and personnel to try and block the Serb forces that were coming from the south, towards the north, threatening the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you stand up and look at the map, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E. If the camera can zoom in immediately. If you can point to the approximate position of the blocking position.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you could hold the pointer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is pointing to a position just below the yellow circle marked "H" within the Srebrenica enclave, and to the right of where it's stated in blue "UN Bravo Company".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain van Duijn, you can sit down now. Thank you. Now, you said in your evidence that you were blocking the Serb forces that were coming from the south, towards the north, and threatening the city of Srebrenica. Why did you need to block the Serb forces that were advancing on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was an order of my captain, Captain Matthijssen, who had ordered me to go south to help the Bravo Company, because of the Serb forces that were engaging and coming in a northern direction, threatening the city where all the Muslim refugees were living. At that time, we didn't know what was going on. There was a lot of shelling going on in that period, so we were afraid that also the city would fall into the hands of the Serbs. And together with air attacks, we would try to block the Serb forces that were coming from the south, to the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges the scene that you saw on the 10th of July in Srebrenica, whilst you were at the blocking position?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We were standing near the APC and there was shelling going on. Most of the time, there was shelling over our heads, on the city itself. We could see smoke coming out of the houses; we could sometimes see the shelling hitting the houses of the town of Srebrenica. At one point -- sometimes the shelling would also be directed at us and near the APCs; you could hear it on the sides of the APCs as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that you were there to protect the refugees in Srebrenica. Can you explain to the Judges the state of the refugees that you saw and what they were doing at this time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: They were very scared, of course, by the shelling. They were fleeing towards the north, towards the UN compounds, because that basically was the only safe place in the enclave left. They were panicked. There was total chaos. They tried to get whatever they had left to take with them and move to the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were at the blocking position, did you see any members of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you saw?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We saw a few soldiers in the vicinity of our location, threatening with rocket launchers to shoot our APCs if we would leave that location. And there were a few soldiers as well, when they also retreated to the north, who were not helping the refugees that tried to flee to the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were these Bosnian Muslim soldiers threatening to shoot at your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Because they wanted us to stay there and remain in the blocking position and also fight against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at what period in time you left this blocking position?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was during the afternoon of the 10th, I think that was, and we left because all of the refugees had left there. The whole part of the town, the southern part of the town, was left by all the people that had lived there. So there was no reason for us to stay there, because we had poor sight of the vicinity. So we retreated towards the UN compound, to see if we could help there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that the town had -- essentially all of the people had left the town. Can you describe the scene, as you saw it, when you left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was totally abandoned, there was no one left there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you moved back yourself to the UN compound, did you see anything on the road between Srebrenica and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I saw some people sitting by the side of the road, and we tried to take as many of the refugees that were sitting alongside of the road, to take them with us, on top of the APC or inside the APC. There were some personal belongings scattered on the sides of the roads, but I didn't see specific things on the road itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can now move to the night of the 11th and 12th of July of 1995. Can you tell the Judges where you were at that time and what happened during that evening?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
