utterances.text: We went to a point we called "point 02," that's the road that goes towards the town of Susnjari, and we took a position there to wait for the coming of the APC of Sergeant Mulder, who had been at OP Mike, observation post Mike, and who was retreating, together with a lot of refugees. And we had to take position there, at first at point 02 itself, and later on a little bit more to the north, near the factory sites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just get up and show on the map the point which is "02" so as to orientate the Judges.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: This is point 02 [indicates], OP Mike, and the road from Susnjari to point O2 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just hold the pointer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness is pointing, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E, to the intersection of the road coming from Susnjari to the road that runs from Bratunac down to Zeleni Jadar, and this is a T-junction next to a violet or purple-coloured triangle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain van Duijn. You can please take a seat. Do you recall the arrival of Sergeant Mulder in his APC?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was late at night, about 10.00 or 11.00 in the evening, and he was standing with his APC on the road. Our APCs were alongside the road, and he was standing in the middle of that, and his APC was covered with refugees, and a lot of refugees followed in the trail of the APC. We took about half an hour or 45 minutes to get everyone off and out of the APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can now move to the morning of the 12th of July, and if you can tell the Judges what you saw that morning.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That morning we heard, by radio, that Serb forces were walking past the fences of the UN compound, and by order of Captain Groen, who was at my location, we put all the weapons we had, small-calibre weapons, inside one APC, and we lifted the .50-calibre machine-guns from the APCs towards the skies, and we saw the Serb forces coming towards our location on the road, and another group of Serb soldiers through the fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you rise, please, Captain van Duijn, and show, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E, the direction that you could see Bosnian Serb soldiers coming from that morning.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: [Indicates]. Two soldiers were coming over the road, from north to south, towards my location, between point 02 and the UN base, and another group was coming east of the UN base and walking through the fields towards point 02.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you indicate where you saw the first group? And if you could actually move the pointer up and down, and I will describe.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The first group was on the road, coming towards our location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be right to say that they were coming from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that the witness is indicating, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1E, that the first group of soldiers was walking down the road from the direction of Bratunac, towards the UN base, which is marked with a blue square inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain van Duijn, the second group of soldiers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We saw them -- and I think they passed the UN base on the eastern side, following the fence, because we saw them walking through the fields, south of the UN base, towards 02.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then let the record show that the witness is indicating that the second group of soldiers was walking down the right-hand side of the blue square marked "UN base," down to the bottom of that square, through an area which is green and, I suppose, represents fields around the UN base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain van Duijn. You can sit down. If you recall, do you recall the pattern of the uniform that these Bosnian Serb soldiers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: They had camouflage-pattern uniforms, but together combined with all sorts of pieces of uniforms. They had bandannas on their heads, backpacks on with different colours of camouflage patterns. So all sorts of combined uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the colour of the camouflage, what colour camouflage --

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was green.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was green. Do you recall the first soldiers that actually arrived at your location at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We saw a few of the soldiers combined in that green uniform with bandannas, or with a Serb flag covered around them, and they had backpacks filled with cigarettes and gave them to our soldiers as sort of presents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these Bosnian Serb soldiers do anything after that, after they were handing out these cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The group that came through the fields, and I could see them coming on the road near point 02, and from there on went into the houses that were near point 02, I could see some characters staying on the road and other soldiers entering the houses and coming out of the houses again. I assume that they were looking if the houses were empty or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And point 02 is the point that you indicated on the map next to you earlier.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the houses were nearby to that point.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who those houses belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I suspect to the refugees that used to live there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move ahead in time to later that morning, and I think you met with Groen, the company commander. What conversation did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Captain Groen was at my location, and I asked him if we could do anything at all because we were just standing there, waiting for things to happen, and he told me that we should go on the road to the north, towards the UN base. There would be a big concentration of refugees over there and there would be some UN soldiers there to try and calm them, and he said, "Go over there and maybe you can help the UN soldiers that are over there, on that location," and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was to essentially assist the refugees that were, at that time, spread all over the factory sites and in the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point in time, can you roughly estimate how many refugees there were in and around the compound at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Around the compound, around the factory sites, there must have been 20.000, 30.000 Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/2, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain van Duijn, do you recall the position that you took up on the 12th of July to direct the soldiers that were working among the refugees?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It must have been in this area here [indicates], near the factory sites that were located here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can place your pointer in the centre of where you're marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is marking, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/2, on the road that runs like a ribbon from the north to the south of the photograph, and he's indicating to a point just to the right and below the Express Bus Compound and to the left and below the Zinc Factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Captain van Duijn. We can leave that exhibit on the ELMO. Now, I think at this point you were approached by a member of the VRS; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was a soldier that said he was a captain named Mane, and he said he was in charge of the Serb soldiers that were in that location, on that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So specifically in that particular area of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was a local, sort of, subordinate commander.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Mane say to which unit he belonged?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He said he was a military police which had a sort of liaison with what he called the Drina Wolves, the Drina Corps. He said he wasn't in the Drina Corps, but his military police unit was more or less working together with the Drina Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 71 and then 72, and if 73 and 74 are made ready, then we can move through these photographs quite quickly. Mr. President, these are stills that have been taken from Prosecutor's Exhibit 3. The witness was shown the video prior to his testimony, and he will identify a number of individuals with whom he had dealings or whom he recognises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Captain van Duijn, this first photograph, who are the individuals on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: This is the guy that called himself Captain Mane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who's the individual on the right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that the witness is indicating that the individual on the left is Captain Mane and the individual on the right is the witness, Captain van Duijn. If the witness could be shown the next exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 72.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that individual?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's Mane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Now, did Captain Mane indicate to you who his commander was?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He spoke to me through his interpreter, called Mickey, and he said his commander had a code name over the radio and was called Stalin; at least his code name over the radio was Stalin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As in Joseph Stalin.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: As in Joseph Stalin, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was some kind of military code name that was being used.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That he used over my radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see this individual, Stalin?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I had seen him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know that the man that you saw was Stalin?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Because Mane described him to me as a little man with glasses on, moustache, and he described him in a fashion that I recognised him. I knew that it was the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could then be shown Exhibits 73 and 74.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recognise anybody on that photograph? And again this is from the video that we viewed prior to you testifying.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The person on the right-hand side, with the glasses on, that's the guy with the code name Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that the witness is indicating, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 73, that the individual on the far right of the photograph with a moustache and spectacles is the individual code-named Stalin. Then if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 74.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: This was the guy with the code name Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 74, the individual who is furthest to the left, whose full face can be seen furthest to the left, wearing again either glasses or sunglasses, is the individual with the code name Stalin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody else on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I recognise in the middle General Mladic and two soldiers or three soldiers that were his bodyguards during the visits, and this, of course, is General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 74, that the individual in the foreground and centre of the photograph is General Mladic and that the three soldiers to his right, one of whom is partially blocked by Mladic's own figure, are bodyguards of Mladic who accompanied him at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain van Duijn. Now, are you aware, were you aware at the time, who Stalin was subordinated to, who the commanding officer of Stalin was at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I recall that I'd seen the soldier with the code name Stalin before, together with Major Nikolic. It looked to me that Major Nikolic was the commander of the guy named Stalin because Major Nikolic was in the middle of the road, Stalin was next to him, more or less explaining -- I couldn't understand what they were talking about because they were talking Serbo-Croat -- but it really looked to me like Major Nikolic was more or less inspecting what was going on there and Stalin was telling him about everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it had the appearance to you of a superior and subordinate relationship.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nikolic being the superior --

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Stalin being the subordinate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Stalin being the subordinate. Now, you had conversations with Mane, that can be seen from the photograph. Do you recall the first conversation that you had with Mane?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. He first asked me if I was the commander of the UN troops over there, and I replied that I was; he said that he was the commander, the local commander, over there from the Serb forces. And he said, "Well, the following is going to happen: The refugees are going away by bus, being transported to Tuzla," and there was no discussion about that. Then he said, "Well, there are two options: The first option is that you leave here with all the UN troops, go back to your compound, and we'll take care of transporting our own way; and the second option is that you stay here and stay at this location." And I told him that we would stay and stand in the middle, and then reported to our operations room and to Major Franken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain van Duijn, why did you decide to stay with some of the soldiers from your platoon?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Because I thought that was the best possible way to stand in between the Serb and the Muslim people, the Serb soldiers and the Muslim refugees, to try and help the refugees as much as we could. Later on, Major Franken also gave me the order to give as much humanitarian aid to the refugees as possible, and the only way that we could do that was to literally stand in the middle of the Serb soldiers and the Muslim refugees. It was my vision that if we would leave over there, we could not see what would happen, and being there, literally in the middle, gave us a chance to do something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time, can you recall the condition of the refugees in the immediate vicinity of your location?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: They were very scared, panicked; tried to get to the UN compound, which at that point was close to the refugees, because a lot of the refugees were already on the compound. So they tried to move to the north. They were panicked, they were scared, and they were pressing each other against the soldiers, my soldiers, the UN soldiers, that tried to calm them. People that fell were trampled on. It was a chaotic situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were a very young officer at the time. How did you feel about the situation?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was a terrible scene to be in. I remember that I was speaking to another soldier that was next to me, and before I went to Bosnia I'd seen two films and that really reminded me of those two films, and I had the idea that I was in the middle of a scene that was sort of a combination between the film "Sophie's Choice" and "Schindler's List," and it was a real strange feeling to be in the middle of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the next significant thing that actually happened that day?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: There was a visit of General Mladic. He came with a group of other officers, I guess, because they also had pistols on their hips and were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many other officers were in the group around General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I think there was a number of about eight or ten people that were together with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I showed you a series of photographs prior to your testimony, and this is one that you recognised. Do you recognise any individuals on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I recognise this man [indicates] on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness has identified the man with the sort of orange face and the grey hair on Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at the time what that individual was called?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: No, I didn't know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with whom did you see that individual?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I saw him together with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, can you remember, any of the other officers that were with General Mladic at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you saw General Mladic doing when he arrived at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It looked to me like, more or less, the making of a propaganda film. He was giving out candy and cans with drinks in them, and there was a film crew filming it all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any other VRS officers, not those necessarily in that group, who you spoke with that day?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I spoke with a person, also in military uniform, and when I asked him about his rank and name, he said that he was a colonel named Jankovic, and he told me that he was a logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown tab 11 of Prosecutor's Exhibit 28, which is, I think, 28/13 and 28/13.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These, again, are photographs that I've shown you previously, and you identified this gentleman. While we're waiting for the photograph, Jankovic stated to you that he was a logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's what he said, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify the individuals on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: To the left is General Mladic and to the right is the person that said he was Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to Colonel Jankovic with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that the witness has identified the individual on the right of the photograph with brown hair, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/13, as being Colonel Jankovic, the individual who introduced himself as a logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Jankovic dressed like that at the time that you met him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He was dressed in uniform, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Jankovic appear to be doing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He was walking around, and it looked to me like he was just looking, more or less inspecting if everything went in the fashion he wanted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to him subsequently that day or the next day?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I spoke to him a few times. I saw him about four or five times in a short period of time. And after that, a few days later, after the whole tragedy had taken place, and the day before we left to go back to Zagreb, I saw him together with Colonel Karremans and Major Franken on the UN base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you communicate with him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: In English. He spoke very good English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say to you on the occasions that you met with him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At first, I just asked him, because I was curious what sort of a soldier he was and what rank he had, and he spoke about his factory he had in Belgrade. He said that he had fought in the war earlier on, somewhere in 1992, and that after that he had been occupied with his company in Belgrade. And he joined the army now again and was there as a logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you subsequently speak about with him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We spoke about the terrible situation over there, and he said, "Well, at least you're still alive." It was a very strange way that he said that to me. And in the periods that I saw him later on, he would just point at me and say, "Well, Porucnik," which means first lieutenant, "I see that you're still alive."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So every time he saw you after this, he would greet you with that phrase.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, that very strange phrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think later that day, General Mladic returned, or at least you saw him return. Can you describe to the Judges what you saw him do on that occasion, on the second occasion that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He came up to me and he wanted to speak to me, he wanted to speak to the commander there, which I was at that period of time. He spoke through his interpreter or through -- my interpreter was a Muslim refugee that was normally attached to the Bravo Company but for that period of time was my translator, and he spoke to a few of my soldiers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the time is now 2.30. Do you wish to break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley. So a break until tomorrow, half past nine. Captain, we need to adjourn now, this is according to our schedule, so that you will resume your testimony tomorrow. We hope we are not causing you any inconvenience with this, but that is how we work. Therefore, we shall adjourn until tomorrow, at half past nine, 9.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
